design_detail: Prospective study with a baseline before use: 56 people who use ecstasy, drawn from a Melbourne cross-sectional study of 184, were assessed face to face after at least a week without ecstasy, then by telephone the day after a weekend (Day 1, mostly Sunday) and two days later (Day 3, mostly Tuesday). 35 chose to take ecstasy that weekend and 21 chose not to. Outcomes: Kessler-10 distress (rephrased to the present day), a 1-10 rating of the day's mood, and the depression, anxiety and hostility items of the clinician-rated Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale; self-reported hours and restlessness of sleep, drug use (Timeline Followback) and stressful events. Two-way repeated-measures ANCOVA (group x time) and correlations of mood change with possible risk factors.
can_establish: Whether, against each person's own baseline, people who chose to take ecstasy over a weekend reported more distress or lower mood one and three days later than people from the same group who chose not to, and which self-reported factors went with mood change.
cannot_establish: Causal effects (use was self-chosen and the groups differed in age, sex and other drug use), effects of known MDMA doses (tablets not tested), effects beyond three days, or the absence of a small effect (35 and 21 people, 47 at Day 3).

sample.recruitment: Subsample of a cross-sectional study of 184 people aged 18-35 who had used ecstasy in the past 12 months, recruited in Melbourne through university and dance-music websites, newsletters, magazines, newspapers, flyers in cafes, music stores and dance events, and snowballing; 63 consented, 56 provided follow-up data (pp. 54, 56).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methods: regular ecstasy use (at least monthly over the last six months) and planning to take ecstasy the following week; excluded pregnancy, self-reported psychotic disorder and poor English. Asked to abstain from ecstasy for 7 days, other drugs for 24 h (except tobacco and caffeine) and alcohol for 12 h before baseline (pp. 54, 56). Reimbursed AUD 25 for the baseline interview.
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group 20 men and 15 women, mean age 24.2 (SD 5.2); abstainers 6 men and 15 women, 21.1 (2.1); history of depression or anxiety disorder 20.0% and 19.0%; mostly Caucasian and with post-school education (Table 1, p. 56).
sample.attrition: One ecstasy-group member was not reached on Day 1; on Day 3, 5 of 35 and 4 of 21 were not reached (86% and 81% followed up); 7 of the 63 who consented provided no follow-up (pp. 56, 60).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected community volunteers; the comparison depends on who chose to take ecstasy that weekend. The groups differed in age, sex, duration of ecstasy use and lifetime cocaine and cannabis use (pp. 56-57). The authors note that people with worse mood might have been harder to reach and that abstainers might be more sensitive to after-effects (p. 60).

exposure.measurement: Self-report of tablets taken and of other drugs (Timeline Followback); tablets were not analysed; 91.4% of the ecstasy group rated it highly or definitely likely that they had taken MDMA (pp. 55, 60).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: mean 1.91 tablets (SD 1.23; range 0.5-5) on the night (Day 0); the Day 1 interview came on average 21.74 h (SD 6.64; 12.5-40) after the last tablet (p. 57). Usual pattern (Table 3, p. 57): typical 1.90 tablets per occasion, lifetime mean 422 tablets (SD 1002) in the ecstasy group and 149 (355) in abstainers; about 1.4 days of use in the past month in both groups.
exposure.polysubstance: On Day 0, 30 of 35 in the ecstasy group drank alcohol (mean 9.52 standard drinks) against 10 of 21 abstainers (5.07); cannabis 34.3% against 14.3%; 6 took amphetamines; mean number of substances 2.51 against 0.71 (p<0.001). Between Days 1 and 3 the ecstasy group used more alcohol and cannabis (Table 5, p. 58). Number of substances, Day 0 sleep, age, sex and duration of ecstasy use were entered as covariates.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence before baseline by self-report only; the authors note the baseline questionnaire covered the past week, which may overlap with after-effects of earlier use (p. 60).

comparison.controls: 21 people from the same sample of people who use ecstasy who chose not to take it that weekend, interviewed on the same days.
comparison.matching: None; group differences in age, sex, drug use and Day 0 sleep were handled as covariates.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline mood was measured, which most earlier studies lacked; why people abstained, recent trauma or stress beyond the follow-up, and objective sleep were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Abstainers also used alcohol, cannabis and other drugs (Table 4), but fewer substances that weekend.

outcomes.instruments: Kessler-10 (K10), timeframe changed from the past month to the present day; subjective mood 1 (worst ever) to 10 (best ever); BPRS depression, anxiety and hostility items rated 1-7 by the interviewer; MASQ short form at baseline only; hours of sleep the previous night from reported sleep and wake times minus waking periods, and restlessness of sleep 1-10 compared with normal (pp. 55-56).
outcomes.validity_norms: The K10 cut-off of 17 or more is validated for the past-month version; its use on a present-day version is untested. BPRS reliability is cited for trained raters; follow-up ratings were made by telephone.
outcomes.operationalization: Mood change = baseline score minus Day 1 or Day 3 score (p. 55); clinically significant distress = K10 of 17 or more.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the 10 group comparisons (K10, mood and three BPRS items at Day 1 and Day 3); for the correlation analyses a modified Bonferroni threshold of p = 0.001 was set from the effective number of variables (matSpD) (p. 55).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: one doctoral candidate conducted all interviews and arranged follow-up calls around planned use, so knew who had taken ecstasy.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals. K10: no main effect of group and no group x time interaction; a time effect at Day 1 (F(1,53) = 4.94, p = 0.03, lower distress than baseline) that disappeared with covariates. Subjective mood: no group or group x day effect; lower than baseline at Day 1 (F(1,52) = 4.60, p = 0.04) and Day 3 (F(1,45) = 6.52, p = 0.01) in both groups; the Day 1 effect disappeared after adjusting for Day 0 sleep. BPRS change scores: no group differences (p > 0.05, values not shown). Means in Table 2 (p. 56). Editors' calculation: K10 of 17 or more at Day 3 in 7 of 30 against 2 of 17, Fisher exact p = 0.45.
analysis.covariates: Sex, age, duration of ecstasy use, hours of sleep on the night of use (or before Day 3), and number of substances, entered one at a time or together (pp. 57-58).
analysis.selective_reporting: BPRS results are given only as not significant; correlation results are reported as significant at p = 0.001 or as trends, with some trends at p = 0.01 although trends were defined as p < 0.01.
analysis.power: Not calculated; the authors note that low rates of mood disorder in the sample may have limited power (p. 59).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against their own baseline a week earlier, people who took ecstasy did not differ from people who abstained in distress, mood or clinician-rated symptoms one or three days later; mood ratings fell a little in both groups. The ecstasy group slept about two hours less on the night of use. Across the whole sample, fewer hours of sleep before Day 3 went with a rise in distress and restless sleep with a drop in mood, and in the ecstasy group restless sleep went with a rise in distress; the number of pills, dancing, overheating, sex and baseline mood were not associated with mood change.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that ecstasy use was not associated with subacute depressive, anxiety or aggressive symptoms and that lowered mood was associated instead with sleep (p. 53). This rests on non-significant differences in 56 people, without intervals, so a small effect cannot be excluded; and adjusting for sleep on the night of use removes part of any effect that runs through lost sleep, which ecstasy nights produced (5.9 against 8.1 hours). The discussion is more careful, calling any subacute effects likely modest, naming low power and calling for larger studies (pp. 59-60).

timeline.event: Curran and Travill: field study reporting lower mid-week mood after weekend ecstasy than after a night of drinking, without a pre-use baseline.
Parrott and Lasky: Saturday-night field study with a drug-free baseline, cited by Scott et al. among the studies that found elevated low mood in the following days.

Pirona and Morgan: cited by Scott et al. as finding no difference against an ecstasy-using comparison group on the Beck Depression Inventory, and effects on negative mood that disappeared after adjusting for sleep.
This study: no group difference against ecstasy-using abstainers, with sleep associated with mood change.

replication.where_it_stands: One of the few studies with both a pre-use baseline and a comparison group of people who also use ecstasy. Its null result disagrees with the earlier field studies that compared people who took ecstasy with people who did not use it (as cited, p. 59), and agrees with Pirona and Morgan (2010) as Scott et al. describe it.

funding.funder: The first author held an Australian Postgraduate Award; the project was funded by the School of Psychology and Psychiatry, Monash University; two authors were supported by the Colonial Foundation (p. 60).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author declares no conflict of interest (as printed, in the singular, for four authors) (p. 60).
funding.affiliations_note: Monash University, King's College London, Queensland University of Technology, Turning Point Alcohol and Drug Centre.

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective study of people who use ecstasy, with daily mood ratings from before a planned weekend to a week after, objective sleep measurement (actigraphy), tablet testing, and a comparison group who go out and lose sleep without taking ecstasy, analysed with sleep as a mediator rather than a covariate.

domains.note: Self-chosen exposure; groups differed in age, sex, duration of ecstasy use and other drug use; covariates were added singly or in small sets, and adjusting for sleep after use may remove part of the effect rather than confounding.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-reported tablets of unknown content, though most participants believed they had taken MDMA.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers from a larger study; the authors raise self-selection of abstainers who may be more sensitive to after-effects.
More alcohol and cannabis in the ecstasy group between Days 1 and 3.
16% not reached at Day 3, similar in both groups; those not reached may have felt worse.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-reports and an interviewer who knew the groups; baseline face to face, follow-up by telephone; K10 timeframe changed.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: BPRS values not shown; many correlations, with trends reported at p = 0.01 despite the stated threshold.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A stronger design than earlier field studies because each person had a baseline and the comparison group also used ecstasy, but the exposure was self-chosen, the groups differed, the sample was small and the outcome measures were self-reported. It can be cited for finding no detectable group difference in mood one and three days after ecstasy in this sample, and for the association of poorer sleep with worse mood; not for the absence of an effect or for sleep as the cause.

key_findings.finding: K10: no main effect of group and no group x time interaction; a main effect of time at Day 1 (F(1,53) = 4.94, p = 0.03), with lower distress than at baseline, not significant after covariates (sex, age, Day 0 sleep, number of drugs on Day 0, duration of ecstasy use). The items depressed and nervous did not differ between groups.
key_findings.locator: Results, Group comparisons: mood, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Subjective mood: no group or group x day effect; both groups lower than baseline at Day 1 (F(1,52) = 4.60, p = 0.04) and Day 3 (F(1,45) = 6.52, p = 0.01). The Day 1 time effect remained after adjusting for sex, age or duration of use but not after adjusting for hours of sleep on the night of use; the Day 3 effect did not survive adjustment for age, sleep before Day 3 or other drug use. After covariates there was still no group effect or interaction; an age x time interaction (F(1,51) = 3.93, p = 0.05) indicated lower mood in younger participants, especially at Day 1.
key_findings.locator: Results, Subjective mood paragraph (p. 57, right column, continuing on p. 58, left column)

key_findings.finding: Clinician-rated BPRS depression, anxiety and hostility change scores did not differ between groups (p > 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results, BPRS clinician ratings paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: K10 of 17 or more (clinically significant distress): ecstasy group 5 (14.3%) at baseline, 4 (11.8%) at Day 1, 7 (23.3%) at Day 3; abstainers 4 (19.0%), 3 (14.3%), 2 (11.8%), with one abstainer at 30 or more at Day 3. Not tested statistically.
key_findings.locator: Results, Follow-up mood: clinically significant symptoms (left column)

key_findings.finding: Sleep the night before Day 1: ecstasy group 5.85 h (SD 2.14) against abstainers 8.06 h (1.93), p<0.001; restless sleep 2.85 (2.64) against 3.76 (2.81). The night before Day 3: 7.98 h (1.80) against 7.93 h (2.89); restless sleep 3.14 against 2.94.
key_findings.locator: Table 5, hours of sleep and restless sleep rows

key_findings.finding: Sleep and mood change, alpha 0.001: across the whole sample, hours slept before Day 3 correlated with the Day 3 K10 change score (r = -0.49, p = 0.001), described as fewer hours with more distress, and restless sleep correlated with the Day 3 drop in mood (r = 0.45, p = 0.001); in the ecstasy group, restless sleep correlated with the Day 3 K10 change (r = -0.59, p = 0.001), and restless sleep (r = 0.55, p = 0.002) and fewer hours (r = -0.46, p = 0.01) with a drop in mood at Day 3. Stressful life events were not associated with mood change.
key_findings.locator: Results, Sleep and Stress paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered page. See reporting issues for the direction of the K10 correlations.

key_findings.finding: No association of mood change with the number of tablets taken, total drugs or alcohol and cannabis on Day 0, feeling hot or time spent dancing, rating of the experience, confidence that MDMA was taken, sex, age, past depression or anxiety, or baseline MASQ symptoms; a trend for more substances used between Days 1 and 3 with a drop in mood at Day 3 (r = 0.37, p = 0.01, whole sample; r = 0.55, p = 0.002, ecstasy group).
key_findings.locator: Results, Correlational analyses: demographics, lifetime drug use, Days 0-2 drug use and ecstasy factors (p. 58, right column, to p. 59, left column)

key_findings.finding: Drugs on the night of use (Day 0): alcohol in 30 of 35 in the ecstasy group against 10 of 21 abstainers, with more drinks in the ecstasy group; cannabis 12 against 3; mean number of substances 2.51 against 0.71 (p<0.001). The Day 1 interview came on average 21.74 h after the last tablet. Amounts are in the exposure field.
key_findings.locator: Results, Follow-up drug use and sleep (p. 57, left column); Table 5 (p. 58)

key_findings.finding: Group differences at baseline: the ecstasy group was older (t(54) = -3.07, p = 0.004), more often male (chi-square(1, 56) = 4.31, p = 0.04), had used ecstasy for longer (t(54) = -2.25, p = 0.03) and had more often tried cocaine; no differences on baseline mood, lifetime ecstasy pills, typical dose or time since last use.
key_findings.locator: Results, Sample characteristics and follow-up, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 56, right column, to p. 57)

reporting_issues.issue: With change scores defined as baseline minus follow-up (p. 55), a negative correlation between hours of sleep and the K10 change (r = -0.49) and a positive one between lifetime amphetamine use and the Day 1 K10 change (r = 0.36, p. 58) imply the opposite of the direction the text gives (fewer hours, or more amphetamine use, with more distress), whereas the negative correlation with restless sleep (r = -0.59) matches its text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the K10 change was computed the other way for some analyses or a sign is wrong; the direction of the sleep-distress association should be cited from the text with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 prints 30 of 35 as 87.7%; 30 of 35 is 85.7%. Its footnote defines a standard drinking unit as equivalent to 10 mg of ethanol, a unit error (presumably grams).
Comparisons of alcohol and cannabis between Days 1 and 3 are reported as t(47) (p. 57), but with 30 and 17 people an independent t-test has 45 degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; suggests the analysis used a different n or the df is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion is described as at least monthly ecstasy use over six months (p. 54) and, in the abstract, as use at least once in 12 months (p. 53); Table 3 shows times since last use of up to 120 days in the ecstasy group and 94 in abstainers (p. 57).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample is less regular in its use than the Methods suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says one ecstasy-group member could not be contacted on Day 1 (p. 56) and also that two participants were assessed two days after use because they could not be contacted on Day 1 (p. 57).
reporting_issues.consequence: Day 1 timing differs for some participants; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations at p = 0.01 are reported as trends (p. 59) although trends were defined as p < 0.01 (p. 58); results at p = 0.001 are called significant with alpha set at 0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sleep associations sit at, not below, the authors' own threshold.
